stories.headline: Congress steps up agitation for removal of Chief Election Commissioner
stories.title: Congress steps up agitation for removal of Chief Election Commissioner
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Transport and BC Welfare Minister Ponnam Prabhakar on Tuesday warned that the Congress would not remain silent if eligible voters were denied their fundamental right to vote, even as Telangana Youth Congress cadres staged a protest outside the State Chief Electoral Officer’s office here demanding the removal and arrest of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar.

Speaking to the media at Sriramulapalli in Koheda mandal of Siddipet district, Mr. Prabhakar alleged that votes of poor and eligible people in rural areas were being removed in the name of revision of electoral rolls.
He accused the Election Commission of India (ECI) failing to function independently and alleged that it was acting under the influence of the Centre.

He condemned the detention of Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi during their protest in Delhi against alleged irregularities in the electoral process, describing the action as undemocratic.
He said the Congress would intensify its ‘Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao’ campaign from the village level to protect the voting rights of every citizen.
Meanwhile, Telangana Youth Congress president Jakkidi Shiva Charan Reddy led the protest outside the Telangana CEO’s office and demanded his immediate arrest.
Mr. Reddy alleged that the CEC was acting in the interests of the BJP and RSS and claimed that nearly 14 crore votes had been removed across the country without due procedure.
He said the Youth Congress would organise protests across Telangana seeking the resignation of Mr. Kumar.
He warned that the agitation would be intensified if the Centre failed to respond to their demands.
Separately, leaders of INDIA bloc parties staged a protest outside the Hyderabad Collectorate demanding the removal and arrest of Mr. Kumar.
They submitted a representation to the Joint Collector and said their agitation would continue until the CEC was removed and a thorough investigation ordered.

Meanwhile, Congress Khairatabad district president M. Rohit, Secunderabad district president Deepak Jain, MLC Kodandaram, CPI State leader Narasimha, CPI(M) city secretary Venkatesh, Telangana Jana Samithi (TJS) leaders Salim Pasha and Arun Kumar, Hyderabad district president Narsaiah and representatives of the VCK participated in the protest.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Stays Demolition Of CSI Church Built As Community Hall In Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi District
stories.title: Supreme Court Stays Demolition Of CSI Church Built As Community Hall In Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi District
stories.summary: The Collector had refused to recognise the community hall as a place of worship citing communal tensions between Hindu and Christian residents.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Collector had refused to recognise the community hall as a place of worship citing communal tensions between Hindu and Christian residents.

The Supreme Court on Friday (October 16) stayed the demolition of a Church of South India (CSI) church in Thippanampatti village in Tamil Nadu's Tenkasi district, in a plea challenging the High Court order finding the structure unauthorised and ordering its restoration as a community hall.
A bench of Justice Vikram Nath, Justice R Mahadevan and Justice Aparesh Singh issued notice on the plea filed by the church trust.
Senior Advocate Huzefa Ahmadi appeared for the church trust.

The case concerns a building constructed by the Tirunelveli Diocesan Trust Association, which was granted permission in 2014 to construct a community hall called the “Church of South India Community Hall”.
The association contends that the building has since been used as a church by the local Christian community, with regular prayers and religious services being conducted peacefully.
The Trust on March 4, 2024, sought recognition of the community hall as a place of worship and permission for the church tower.
However, the District Collector rejected the application on June 25, 2024, refusing permission to convert the community hall into a church and to construct the tower.
The Collector's decision was challenged by the Trust before the Madras High Court.
Before the High Court, the State argued that the original permission covered only a community hall and no approval had been obtained for a spire erected on the building.

Relying on Rule 4(3) of the Tamil Nadu Panchayats Building Rules, 1997, the State submitted that prior approval of the District Collector was mandatory for a site intended to be used for public worship or religious purposes.
The rule permits the Collector to refuse approval if the proposed use is likely to endanger public peace and order.

stories.headline: India’s blind women cricketers still wait for house sites and jobs a year after their World Cup win
stories.title: India’s blind women cricketers still wait for house sites and jobs a year after their World Cup win
stories.summary: Captain Deepika T.C. of Madakasira in Andhra Pradesh’s Sri Sathya Sai district is still waiting for the house site she was promised
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'world cup' in title weight 42
article_sentences: Deepika T.C. captained India to victory in the first Women’s T20 World Cup for the Blind in November 2025.
Nearly a year later, she is still waiting for the house site that leaders and officials promised her.
She and her 15 teammates, who won the tournament hosted jointly by India and Sri Lanka, say they are unable to get the support they need from society and the government in their day-to-day lives.
They do not get playgrounds and fitness guidance in their localities, and they cannot afford training in big cities.
Leaders who make tall promises in public have shown little interest in ensuring government jobs and house sites for them, they said.
Ms. Deepika hails from Madakasira in Sri Sathya Sai district.
“Due to our partial vision issues, we cannot move around government offices to follow up on house site issues.
The government has to do its own and instill confidence among us,” she told.
The Hindu.
Ms. Deepika, who developed vision problems as an infant, completed a degree course and focused on cricket in spite of her family’s financial struggles.
Her parents, Timmappa and Chittemma, encouraged her to practise cricket in Bengaluru although they had many fears about her partial vision.
She has been consistently playing well and won special recognition when she scored 92 runs off 45 balls against Australia in a World Cup match.

stories.headline: India Cements acquires 3.6% stake in Zenataris Renewable for captive power needs
stories.title: India Cements acquires 3.6% stake in Zenataris Renewable for captive power needs
stories.summary: The consideration involved is an equity investment of over Rs ₹20 crore and it will be closed within 120 days from the execution of the agreement
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India Cements on Thursday said that the company has entered into energy supply and share subscription agreement to acquire 3.62 per cent equity shares of Zenataris Renewable Energy Private Ltd, a company engaged in generation and transmission of renewable energy.

“The acquisition is for the purposes of meeting India Cements’ green energy needs, optimising energy cost and comply with regulatory requirements for captive power consumption under electricity laws,” the company said in a filing to the exchanges.
The consideration involved is an equity investment of over ₹20 crore and it will be closed within 120 days from the execution of the agreement.

Zenataris is based in Hyderabad, and is a special purpose vehicle (SPV) established for the development and operation of Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) hybrid renewable energy project located at Kudligi, Vijayanagara District, Karnataka.
The SPV shall supply 11 MW renewable energy to the cement plants of India Cements on a group captive basis, a statement filed by India Cements to the exchanges said.

stories.headline: India's $100 billion China trade deficit: Are non-tariff barriers blocking Indian exports?
stories.title: India's $100 billion China trade deficit: Are non-tariff barriers blocking Indian exports?
stories.summary: Speaking at an interaction in Bangkok, Sitharaman said China's restrictions were preventing Indian products from realising their potential in one of the world's largest markets.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: “With China, I think our trade balance is against us, and it is growing exponentially,” Sitharaman said.
She added that China “uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly” and that this was “the biggest hurdle in the in the trade between India and China.”
Sitharaman pointed to phytosanitary regulations, which are intended to prevent the spread of plant pests and diseases, as one of the barriers affecting Indian exporters.
She said Indian products, including generic medicines, beef and vegetables, had “immense” potential in the Chinese market but faced restrictions.
Non-tariff barriers can include licensing requirements, product standards, testing procedures and sanitary or phytosanitary measures.

While such regulations can serve legitimate health and safety objectives, differences in implementation and market-access requirements can increase compliance costs and make it harder for exporters to enter foreign markets.
For Indian businesses, improving access to China could create opportunities across pharmaceuticals and agricultural products.

However, the extent to which these barriers account for the trade deficit would need to be assessed alongside other factors, including the competitiveness of Indian products and the composition of bilateral trade.
Sitharaman said India had refrained from imposing retaliatory non-tariff restrictions or countervailing duties on Chinese goods, despite the widening imbalance.

The finance minister's remarks come as New Delhi and Beijing seek to stabilise relations following the border confrontation in 2020, which triggered prolonged diplomatic tensions and restrictions on Chinese investments and business activities.
Both countries have since taken steps to ease tensions and resume high-level engagement.
However, trade remains a contentious area, with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar also recently saying India was not “getting a level playing field in China.”

stories.headline: Kashmir Syncretic Traditions
stories.title: Kashmir Syncretic Traditions
stories.summary: Since time immemorial, Kashmir has been the abode of many deities, Sufi saints, seers, and savants of very high spiritual splendour, intensity, and grace who enriched the culture and thought process of the people. The land has been blessed by deities Lord Shiva, Parvati, Brahma, Vishnu, Lord Ram, Sita, and Lord Krishna. Sufi saints and Rishis Lal Ded, Nund Rishi, Shah Hamdani, and Sayed Sharaf-ud-Din Rehman (Bulbul Shah) advocated the oneness of God and brotherhood through divine preachings. Kashmir has also been blessed by the Sikh Gurus, Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, and Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, who also carried the same message. Buddhist monastic Guru Padmasambhav also preached in Kashmir. These noble men believed in the magnanimity of God and spread the message of universal brotherhood. Rishi Kashyap bifurcated a mountain at village Khadniyar, Baramulla, and drained Lake Sati Sar, and as a result, the Valley emerged. The Valley experiences picturesque frames in various seasons, each having its exquisite aroma. God has sanctified all the beauty of nature in the Valley, and Kashmir is indeed the Divine Land, whose beauty takes heavenly shades, from blooming spring flowers to golden autumn leaves. Kashmir, also in all its feminine beauty of crystal -clear streams and lakes, lush green valleys, and magnificent snow-capped Himalayan peaks, qualifies for the title “Paradise on Earth.” Sanskrit poet Kalidasa has written about the Valley: “The place is more beautiful than heaven and is the benefactor of Supreme bliss and happiness. It seems to me that I am taking a bath in the lake of Nectar.” Kashmir has the distinction of being home to many revered Islamic shrines, ancient Hindu temples, and historical Sikh Gurdwaras that reflect a rich example of spiritual harmony. Syncretic traditions are cultural, religious, architectural, and philosophical practices that blend different and distinct belief systems into a new, unified whole. The history of Kashmir is not adequately understood through the background of any particular religion. It is rather the history of a civilization repeatedly shaped over many centuries. The Kashmir Valley became a meeting ground of religious traditions, philosophical systems, languages, political cultures, and social practices. Brahminical traditions, Buddhism, Kashmir Shaivism, Islam, Sufism, Rishism, and later Sikh and Dogra influences did not suddenly appear one after another and disappear. They interacted with what already existed. Elements were absorbed, transformed, resisted, adapted, and sometimes rejected. Once Islam became indigenous to Kashmir, it itself underwent transformation through its encounter with the same local cultural environment. That is where Sufism and, particularly, the Rishi traditions became central. Sayed Ali Hamdani was the greatest missionary, whose personality wielded the most extraordinary influence in the spread of Islam. Sikhism did not become a demographic equivalent o f Islam or the older Hindu traditions of Kashmir, but Sikh institutions, communities, and political authority became part of Kashmir’s evolving social landscape. During the Dogra rule, the political structure changed, administrative institutions changed, and relations among religious communities acquired a new political dimension. The celestial Valley, cradled in its arms, a unique type of Hindu Mysticism and Muslim Sufism. Mysticism in Kashmir was always different; there were Hindu mystics whose principles and methods resembled or were identical to those of Muslim saints. Also, there had been Muslim Rishis who were influenced by Kashmir Shaivism and Hindu thought. Four major Sufi “Silsilas” or orders that obtained prominence between the 12th and 16th centuries were: • Qadiri Order, founded by Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad • Suharwardiya Order, founded by Shihab-al-Din Suharwardi of Persia • Shadhiliya Order, founded by Abu -al-Hasan-al-Shadhili, a Moroccan scholar • Mevlevi Order, founded by Jalal -al-Din Muhammad Rumi, resident of Wakhsh, present-day Tajikistan Another faith that evolved was Rishism. A Rishi is a sage who sees spiritual truth. Abul Fazal writes, “The most respected class of people in this country, Kashmir, is the Rishis.” Although they have not abandoned the traditional and customary form of Taqlid (following), yet they are true in their worship. Emperor Jahangir wrote, “Although they have not acquired learning and Marifa, they live a frank and unostentatious life.” The Islamic philosophy of divine unity of being (Wahdat -ul-Wujud) is not different from Hindu philosophy of non -duality (Advaita). It is not at all surprising that the Rishis constantly preached complete harmony amongst different religions and peace and understanding among their followers. If Lal Ded represents the pre-Islamic spiritual inheritance of Kashmir, Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani (Nund Rishi) represents the extraordinary localisation of Islam. Linguistic syncretism connects people and ideas. Language is the core text of human life that lets us shape thoughts, build societies, and pass down knowledge across time. All faiths in Kashmir, over the entire spectrum of time, spoke the same language, “Koshur.” The Muslim and Hindu communities wore the same dress, “Pheran,” shared common surnames, had some common wedding rituals like the use of Mehendi (Henna), and referred to the bride and groom as Maharein and Mahraz. The communities together engaged in the same music and dance (Rouf, Chakri, Band Pathar). Sufi Mystical Music of Kashmir (SAMA) forms an essential part of the region’s rich mystic and classical traditions called Sufiana Kalam. The lyrics used include Hamd (Praise of God), Na’d (Cosmic sound or Divine Vibration), and mystical poetry of Kashmiri saints. The main instruments used are Santoor, Rubab, and Trumbkanari. Hindus and Muslims together participated in many religious functions. Zain -ul- Abdin participated in the festival of Vyeth Truva (ceremony marking the birth of River Jhelum). Historically, both communities carried out shrine veneration and frequented shrines of Sufi mystics and Rishis, blending Vedantic/Shaivite philosophy with Islamic Sufism. The day after the festival of Herath (Mahashivratri), Muslim neighbours traditionally visited Pandit households to offer greetings and exchange pleasantries (a custom named SALAM), symbolising communal harmony. During the Afghan rule, Jabbar Khan wanted to test the local belief that on Shivratri there is a likelihood of snowfall. He banned the celebration in the scheduled month of February and forced the community to hold it in June/July. To his shock and dismay, it snowed in the Valley on that summer day. The architectural fusion of Kashmir not only represents the adaptation of Islamic principles to local conditions but also underscores the spirit of tolerance and coexistence that has historically defined Kashmiri society. Some of the shrines, often built in a combination of Islamic and Hindu architectural styles, stand as symbols of the harmony that the Rishis sought to create in Kashmir. The wooden structure of Khanqah, adorned with intricate papier-mâché work, colourful floral motifs, and stunning wood carving, as also the magnificent Jama Masjid, are the finest examples of Syncretic Kashmiri Islamic Architecture. The indigenous secularism, traditional composite culture, and social ethos of Kashmir represented communal harmony, religious tolerance, and shared heritage among its people. Though presently people connect with the word Kashmiriyat, this word does not find mention in any important historical accounts. It was sometime in 1975, after the Kashmir Accord, that Mohd Amin (Ibn Mahjoor) had proposed that we must support a political party that is rooted in Kashmir and would retain the culture of Kashmir, and that would be Kashmiriyat. Kashmiriyat and the composite culture got threatened during the armed militancy when the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits took place on 19 January. The word Kashmiriyat has often been quoted in various debates and conferences. Kashmiris have always resisted external aggression that started with the invasion by the Mughals, but what has been more painful is that the nefarious designs during militancy were not understood. With the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits, Kashmiryat and composite culture have taken a huge hit, but all-out efforts are being taken to see to it that this cementing force is not threatened anymore. The militancy in Kashmir affected people of every faith, and tens of thousands of innocent lives were lost. More than 150 Hindu shrines across the Valley were damaged, desecrated, or left in ruins. The terrorist strikes in the Valley did not even spare holy shrines. Foreign terrorist Mast Gul and his men established a retreat near the holy Charar -e-Sharif shrine. The siege lasted for more than 60 days. The siege ended on 11 May 1995 with a fire that engulfed the shrine. 1990. To conclude, Kashmir’s Syncretic traditions were not created by a proclamation. They emerged gradually from centuries of human interaction. The Valley went through a trying time during the militancy period, and it was these traditions and values that helped Kashmir to emerge a winner, embracing people of all faiths. The manner in which people of all faiths stood by each other in total sync and harmony to fight the floods of 2014 was again a great example of Kashmiryat. Gurdwaras, Mosques, and Temples were open to people of all faiths for food and shelter. The efforts being taken for a dignified and secure return of the Kashmiri Pandits are a welcome step to revive the Syncretic Traditions of Kashmir. opening: Since time immemorial, Kashmir has been the abode of many deities, Sufi saints, seers, and savants of very high spiritual splendour, intensity, and grace who enriched the culture and thought process of the people.
The land has been blessed by deities Lord Shiva, Parvati, Brahma, Vishnu, Lord Ram, Sita, and Lord Krishna.
body: Sufi saints and Rishis Lal Ded, Nund Rishi, Shah Hamdani, and Sayed Sharaf-ud-Din Rehman (Bulbul Shah) advocated the oneness of God and brotherhood through divine preachings.
Kashmir has also been blessed by the Sikh Gurus, Guru Nanak Dev Ji, Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, and Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, who also carried the same message.
Buddhist monastic Guru Padmasambhav also preached in Kashmir.
These noble men believed in the magnanimity of God and spread the message of universal brotherhood.
Rishi Kashyap bifurcated a mountain at village Khadniyar, Baramulla, and drained Lake Sati Sar, and as a result, the Valley emerged.
The Valley experiences picturesque frames in various seasons, each having its exquisite aroma.
God has sanctified all the beauty of nature in the Valley, and Kashmir is indeed the Divine Land, whose beauty takes heavenly shades, from blooming spring flowers to golden autumn leaves.

Kashmir, also in all its feminine beauty of crystal -clear streams and lakes, lush green valleys, and magnificent snow-capped Himalayan peaks, qualifies for the title “Paradise on Earth.” Sanskrit poet Kalidasa has written about the Valley: “The place is more beautiful than heaven and is the benefactor of Supreme bliss and happiness.

It seems to me that I am taking a bath in the lake of Nectar.” Kashmir has the distinction of being home to many revered Islamic shrines, ancient Hindu temples, and historical Sikh Gurdwaras that reflect a rich example of spiritual harmony.
Syncretic traditions are cultural, religious, architectural, and philosophical practices that blend different and distinct belief systems into a new, unified whole.
The history of Kashmir is not adequately understood through the background of any particular religion.
It is rather the history of a civilization repeatedly shaped over many centuries.
The Kashmir Valley became a meeting ground of religious traditions, philosophical systems, languages, political cultures, and social practices.
Brahminical traditions, Buddhism, Kashmir Shaivism, Islam, Sufism, Rishism, and later Sikh and Dogra influences did not suddenly appear one after another and disappear.
They interacted with what already existed.
Elements were absorbed, transformed, resisted, adapted, and sometimes rejected.
Once Islam became indigenous to Kashmir, it itself underwent transformation through its encounter with the same local cultural environment.
That is where Sufism and, particularly, the Rishi traditions became central.
Sayed Ali Hamdani was the greatest missionary, whose personality wielded the most extraordinary influence in the spread of Islam.

Sikhism did not become a demographic equivalent o f Islam or the older Hindu traditions of Kashmir, but Sikh institutions, communities, and political authority became part of Kashmir’s evolving social landscape.
During the Dogra rule, the political structure changed, administrative institutions changed, and relations among religious communities acquired a new political dimension.
The celestial Valley, cradled in its arms, a unique type of Hindu Mysticism and Muslim Sufism.
Mysticism in Kashmir was always different; there were Hindu mystics whose principles and methods resembled or were identical to those of Muslim saints.
Also, there had been Muslim Rishis who were influenced by Kashmir Shaivism and Hindu thought.

Four major Sufi “Silsilas” or orders that obtained prominence between the 12th and 16th centuries were: • Qadiri Order, founded by Sheikh Abdul Qadir Gilani of Baghdad • Suharwardiya Order, founded by Shihab-al-Din Suharwardi of Persia • Shadhiliya Order, founded by Abu -al-Hasan-al-Shadhili, a Moroccan scholar • Mevlevi Order, founded by Jalal -al-Din Muhammad Rumi, resident of Wakhsh, present-day Tajikistan Another faith that evolved was Rishism.
A Rishi is a sage who sees spiritual truth.

Abul Fazal writes, “The most respected class of people in this country, Kashmir, is the Rishis.” Although they have not abandoned the traditional and customary form of Taqlid (following), yet they are true in their worship.

Emperor Jahangir wrote, “Although they have not acquired learning and Marifa, they live a frank and unostentatious life.” The Islamic philosophy of divine unity of being (Wahdat -ul-Wujud) is not different from Hindu philosophy of non -duality (Advaita).
It is not at all surprising that the Rishis constantly preached complete harmony amongst different religions and peace and understanding among their followers.
If Lal Ded represents the pre-Islamic spiritual inheritance of Kashmir, Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Noorani (Nund Rishi) represents the extraordinary localisation of Islam.
Linguistic syncretism connects people and ideas.
Language is the core text of human life that lets us shape thoughts, build societies, and pass down knowledge across time.

All faiths in Kashmir, over the entire spectrum of time, spoke the same language, “Koshur.” The Muslim and Hindu communities wore the same dress, “Pheran,” shared common surnames, had some common wedding rituals like the use of Mehendi (Henna), and referred to the bride and groom as Maharein and Mahraz.
The communities together engaged in the same music and dance (Rouf, Chakri, Band Pathar).
Sufi Mystical Music of Kashmir (SAMA) forms an essential part of the region’s rich mystic and classical traditions called Sufiana Kalam.
The lyrics used include Hamd (Praise of God), Na’d (Cosmic sound or Divine Vibration), and mystical poetry of Kashmiri saints.
The main instruments used are Santoor, Rubab, and Trumbkanari.
Hindus and Muslims together participated in many religious functions.
Zain -ul- Abdin participated in the festival of Vyeth Truva (ceremony marking the birth of River Jhelum).
Historically, both communities carried out shrine veneration and frequented shrines of Sufi mystics and Rishis, blending Vedantic/Shaivite philosophy with Islamic Sufism.

The day after the festival of Herath (Mahashivratri), Muslim neighbours traditionally visited Pandit households to offer greetings and exchange pleasantries (a custom named SALAM), symbolising communal harmony.
During the Afghan rule, Jabbar Khan wanted to test the local belief that on Shivratri there is a likelihood of snowfall.
He banned the celebration in the scheduled month of February and forced the community to hold it in June/July.
To his shock and dismay, it snowed in the Valley on that summer day.

The architectural fusion of Kashmir not only represents the adaptation of Islamic principles to local conditions but also underscores the spirit of tolerance and coexistence that has historically defined Kashmiri society.
Some of the shrines, often built in a combination of Islamic and Hindu architectural styles, stand as symbols of the harmony that the Rishis sought to create in Kashmir.

The wooden structure of Khanqah, adorned with intricate papier-mâché work, colourful floral motifs, and stunning wood carving, as also the magnificent Jama Masjid, are the finest examples of Syncretic Kashmiri Islamic Architecture.
The indigenous secularism, traditional composite culture, and social ethos of Kashmir represented communal harmony, religious tolerance, and shared heritage among its people.
Though presently people connect with the word Kashmiriyat, this word does not find mention in any important historical accounts.

It was sometime in 1975, after the Kashmir Accord, that Mohd Amin (Ibn Mahjoor) had proposed that we must support a political party that is rooted in Kashmir and would retain the culture of Kashmir, and that would be Kashmiriyat.
Kashmiriyat and the composite culture got threatened during the armed militancy when the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits took place on 19 January.
The word Kashmiriyat has often been quoted in various debates and conferences.
Kashmiris have always resisted external aggression that started with the invasion by the Mughals, but what has been more painful is that the nefarious designs during militancy were not understood.
With the exodus of Kashmiri Pandits, Kashmiryat and composite culture have taken a huge hit, but all-out efforts are being taken to see to it that this cementing force is not threatened anymore.
The militancy in Kashmir affected people of every faith, and tens of thousands of innocent lives were lost.
More than 150 Hindu shrines across the Valley were damaged, desecrated, or left in ruins.
The terrorist strikes in the Valley did not even spare holy shrines.
Foreign terrorist Mast Gul and his men established a retreat near the holy Charar -e-Sharif shrine.
The siege lasted for more than 60 days.
The siege ended on 11 May 1995 with a fire that engulfed the shrine.
To conclude, Kashmir’s Syncretic traditions were not created by a proclamation.
They emerged gradually from centuries of human interaction.
The Valley went through a trying time during the militancy period, and it was these traditions and values that helped Kashmir to emerge a winner, embracing people of all faiths.
The manner in which people of all faiths stood by each other in total sync and harmony to fight the floods of 2014 was again a great example of Kashmiryat.
Gurdwaras, Mosques, and Temples were open to people of all faiths for food and shelter.
The efforts being taken for a dignified and secure return of the Kashmiri Pandits are a welcome step to revive the Syncretic Traditions of Kashmir.
